title: Arguing a position
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: at + V (an objection in another voice)

rules.text: dēnique CLOSES AN ARGUMENT WHERE L2-M10's postrēmō CLOSES A STORY. prīmum, deinde, dēnique is the classical three-part structure and both third members mean 'finally' — the difference is REGISTER, and a learner who ends an argument with postrēmō has told a story instead. The first two are shared, which is why only one word is new.

at INTRODUCES SOMEBODY ELSE's OBJECTION IN THEIR VOICE, AND L1-M9's sed DOES NOT. sed is the neutral 'but' and joins two things the speaker says; at hands the floor to an opponent for one clause — 'but, you will say'. So a Latin argument can raise an objection without anybody else being in the room, and the word does all of that work. It comes FIRST in its clause.

immō DOES NOT MERELY DENY: IT RAISES. 'Not only not difficult — necessary' is the full force of it, and English needs a phrase. Against L1-M2's minimē, which denies flatly, immō corrects UPWARDS — and it comes first in its clause, like at, itaque, ergō, ideō and the three sequencers. SEVEN WORDS COME FIRST AND SIX COME SECOND, and by the fiftieth module that list is the only useful form of the rule.

THE ABLATIVE ABSOLUTE ARRIVES, AND L4-M2 AND L4-M4 BOTH WANTED IT. Two words in the ablative do the work of an English clause — hīs rēbus dictīs, 'these things having been said', which covers 'when', 'since' and 'after' all at once — with NO VERB AND NO CONJUNCTION. The case is the connection, which makes it the most compressed construction in the language and the reason it belongs in an argument. Its one real error is writing the nominative instead, which leaves two words dangling with nothing to attach them.

quod sī IS TWO TAUGHT WORDS MEANING SOMETHING NEITHER MEANS ALONE — 'and if, but if' — and it is the ONLY place this course writes quod outside L1-M9's 'because'. The key is shared, so this row names both readings, which is the remedy L4-M6's cum rows use on its fourth outing. And dīc drops its ending: it is one of exactly four Latin imperatives that do — dīc, dūc, fac, fer.

nēmō nōn IS A REAL IDIOM AND IT MEANS 'EVERYBODY'. M5's plate warned that adding nōn to nēmō cancels the negative; here the cancelling IS the point, and a rhetorical close is exactly where a Roman used it. The same two words are a mistake in one module and a device in the next, and only the intention differs — which is as good a definition of rhetoric as this course can give.

AN ARGUMENT IS CARRIED BY ITS CONNECTIVES AND NOT BY ITS GRAMMAR. S10 is a whole case — three steps, an objection, a correction, an absolute and a close — and the only new construction in it is the ablative absolute. Everything else has been available for at least five modules and most of it since L2, which is what a sixth module of a fifth level should feel like: arranging what forty-nine rungs have supplied.
